Q: Why do I get a TypeError when indexing a dictionary .items() result? A:

my_dict = {"key1": "value1", "key2": "value2"}

l = list(my_dict.items())

print(l[0]) # ('key1', 'value1')

Q: How to parse JSON in Kotlin A:

The best and quick practice is instead of manually checking for each key, generate native Kotlin "data classes" using tools e.g. https://json2kotlin.com

So your API response turns into the following couple of data classes corresponding to the JSON structure:

data class Json4Kotlin_Base (

    val users : List<Users>
)

and

data class Users (

    val id : String,
    val name : String,
    val age : Int,
    val gender : String,
    val email : Email
)

and

data class Email (

    val primary : String,
    val secondary : String
)

When you get the result, you simple map the JSON response to these data classes. The video here shows how to do it step by step, and includes more sample code.

Q: How to fetch Sharepoint data and load into Azure Blob Storage using Azure Data Factory? A:

Instead of OData, You can also use SharePoint REST API Directly.

Obtain the REST API endpoint for your SharePoint data. Generally, it looks like: https://<your-domain>.sharepoint.com/sites/<site-name>/_api/web/lists/getbytitle('<List Name>')/items.

Create Linked Services in Azure Data Factory. HTTP Linked Service using the Base URL (SharePoint REST endpoint). Use 'Basic' or another suitable authentication method.

Create a New Dataset, For SharePoint, select the HTTP dataset type. Configure it to use the HTTP Linked Service you created. Specify the relative URL if needed, and other configurations.

Now you can use a Copy Data Pipeline. For the source, select the SharePoint datase. For the destination, select the Azure Blob Storage dataset and Map the fields if necessary.

SharePoint REST API has limitations on the number of items returned in one request, so you might have to handle pagination if you're working with large lists.

Q: Query tuning: counting distinct matching rows across tables A:

For best performance I would recommend the following indexes:

CREATE INDEX index_name ON ShortPricePaidData2024(county, PAON, street, city)
CREATE INDEX index_name ON ShortPricePaidData2025(county, PAON, street, city)

or similar indexes with the same first four columns (in any order).

These indexes would allow the query execution plan to eliminate duplicates and match rows from both sources using a merge-join without any additional sort operations.

See this db<>fiddle that shows execution plans both without and with indexes. The execution with indexes is significantly better.

I also considered the following two queries that deferred the DISTINCT and used an EXISTS() test or source table JOIN to check for matches. The first has performance similar to your original query. The latter results in a loop-join with poorer performance. Both are included in the above fiddle.

-- Similar performance
SELECT 
    pBoth.county, 
    COUNT(*) AS properties_sold_both_years
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT p24.county, p24.PAON, p24.street, p24.city
    FROM ShortPricePaidData2024 p24
    WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT *
        FROM ShortPricePaidData2025 p25
        WHERE p25.county = p24.county
        AND p25.PAON     = p24.PAON
        AND p25.street   = p24.street
        AND p25.city     = p24.city
    )
) pBoth
GROUP BY pBoth.county;

-- Poorer performance
SELECT 
    pBoth.county, 
    COUNT(*) AS properties_sold_both_years
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT p24.county, p24.PAON, p24.street, p24.city
    FROM ShortPricePaidData2024 p24
    JOIN ShortPricePaidData2025 p25
        ON p25.county  = p24.county
        AND p25.PAON   = p24.PAON
        AND p25.street = p24.street
        AND p25.city   = p24.city
) pBoth
GROUP BY pBoth.county;
